title: How nearly can tetrahedra close up: the exponent
credit: Steinhaus problem; Świerczkowski (1959) non-closure; Elgersma & Wagon (2016), arXiv:1610.00280.
results: g(n) >= c*3^{-n/2} for all n (new, short proof): g_n = s_{i1}...s_{in}, linear part = ±R_q, q = v_{i1}...v_{in}, v_i the pure quaternions ±i±j±k (norm 3); non-backtracking => q primitive in the Hurwitz order (unique factorisation; checked by computer to n=11). If T_n is near T_0 the linear part is near a symmetry ±R_u; q*conj(u) cannot be real (primitivity / 2*3^n not a square), so its vector part has length >=1/2 while |q u| <= sqrt2*3^{n/2}, giving rotation error >> 3^{-n/2}.
premise_risks: QED-internal derivation (unrefereed): the bounds 1/12 ≤ κ ≤ 1/2 (Hurwitz-order primitivity checked by computer only to n = 11). The formal Claim only uses the definitions, not these bounds.
plain: Glue regular tetrahedra face to face in a chain of length n; it can never close exactly. How close to closing can it get? Short arguments show the best gap is at least about 3^{-n/2} and, for infinitely many n, at most about 3^{-n/12}; counting suggests 3^{-n/6}. Narrow the exponent range [1/12, 1/2].
math: Let g(k) be the minimal Hausdorff distance between T_k and T_0 over non-backtracking face-reflection chains of length k, and κ := liminf_{n→∞} −(1/n) log₃ min_{1≤k≤n} g(k). Known: 1/12 ≤ κ ≤ 1/2 (heuristic κ = 1/6). Prove κ > 1/12, i.e. there are δ > 0 and N such that for every n ≥ N some non-backtracking chain of length between 1 and n ends within 3^{−(1/12+δ)n} of T_0.
